description:
ITM (International Tech Machines) is a team project focused on data analysis, machine learning, and hardware/software integration for space exploration.

For the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, we built OUTPOST, a browser game where students plan and run a lunar or Martian outpost using real NASA mission data. Always open to collaborating with educators, game designers and space enthusiasts.
summary: OUTPOST is a free browser game that turns students aged 10–17 into mission planners for a 4-person outpost on the Moon or Mars. Players pack an 8-tonne cargo lander with solar arrays, batteries, fission power, water recycling, oxygen generation, greenhouses, regolith shielding and supplies, then run the base for 60 days through dust storms, the 14.8-day lunar night, solar particle events and equipment failures. Every five days they decide what the crew does and which systems get power. A live engineering check and an end-of-mission debrief explain every outcome with real NASA numbers: BVAD consumption rates, the ISS's 98% water recovery, Curiosity RAD radiation data, MOXIE oxygen production and NASA-STD-3001 dose limits. Three sites (lunar south pole, Jezero Crater on Mars, lunar equator) each break a different system, so students experience firsthand why real missions are designed the way they are. The game needs no install or login, runs on any school laptop, and a shared mission code lets a whole class fly the same mission and compare plans.
details:
What it does. OUTPOST lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost and feel the engineering trade-offs that decide whether a mission succeeds. The game has three phases. In Plan, players spend an 8,000 kg cargo budget on power (solar arrays, batteries, a 10 kWe fission unit), life support (a 93% or 98% water recycler, electrolysis, a MOXIE-class oxygen plant on Mars, an ice-mining rover at the lunar pole), food (packaged supplies, greenhouses), and radiation protection (regolith berms or full cover, a storm shelter). A live engineering check simulates 60 days and warns when oxygen, water or food would run out, when power fails, and whether the habitat meets NASA's 0.8 mSv/day surface design target. In Operate, every 5 days players choose a crew focus (Science EVA, Maintenance, Habitat care, Take shelter) and switch systems on or off while random events arrive: dust storms, terrain shadows, lunar sunset, solar particle events and recycler failures. In Debrief, they get a grade (S–F) and personalised lessons that tie their result to real NASA data, for example why the water ran out or how their crew's dose compares with the 600 mSv career limit.

Why it matters. Space STEM content is usually either oversimplified or built for engineers. OUTPOST sits in between. Each site breaks a different system: radiation at the lunar south pole, weak sunlight and dust on Mars, and the 14.8-day night at the lunar equator. Students therefore discover on their own why NASA chooses the south pole for Artemis, why MOXIE matters, and why fission surface power is being developed.

Tools. HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with SVG graphics and no external libraries; hosted on GitHub Pages. The simulation engine is a pure JavaScript module that also runs in Node.js, which we used for automated balance testing across many random mission seeds.

Creativity and design factors. A seeded mission code gives a whole class identical surprises, so students compare strategies and not luck. Failure explains the engineering instead of only showing "game over". Every number links to its source in an in-game Data Library, and simplified values are clearly labelled "game estimate". The game is lightweight, needs no login and works offline once loaded. It uses no NASA logos or insignia. Next steps: Kazakh and Russian translations, a teacher mode and longer missions.
